title: kv-aware-warmth-manager-and-cache-fencing-prd-sketch
body:
Overview
This document proposes a lightweight PRD for a KV-aware Warmth Manager and Tenant Cache Fencing system to improve latency tail and isolation for Redwood Dedicated pools. The idea: coordinate warm-pool prewarming, KV cache residency, and tenant-level fencing so we can autoscale GPU and memory in ways that respect per-tenant SLOs and reduce noisy-neighbor cache thrashing.

Problem statement
- Observed: cold-starts on large context workloads produce long-tail latency spikes because KV cache misses + model memory cold pages coincide with scaled-up allocation.
- Observed: eviction churn across tenants causes throughput jitter when one tenant’s transient burst evicts hot KV entries for others.
- Current autoscaler lacks cache-awareness and treats memory as fungible; this leads to reactive scaling that misses short microbursts and overprovisions for sustained load.
- Need: predictable latency for latency-sensitive tenants, and better unit economics by avoiding unnecessary over-provision.

Goals
- Latency: reduce p99 generation latency for KV-heavy workloads by 25–50% in typical microburst scenarios.
- Isolation: provide soft fencing for per-tenant KV residency to avoid cross-tenant thrash during bursts.
- Efficiency: reduce warm-start GPU time and redundant model load operations by coordinating warm-pool lifecycle with KV heat.
- Ops: expose clear telemetry and runbook for warm-pool behavior and fence events; enable gradual rollout.

Non-goals
- Not attempting to replace full tenant billing/credit systems (this sits orthogonal to burst-credit work).
- Not a complete replacement for existing eviction or preemption primitives; it layers on top and integrates with them.

High-level approach
1) KV heat signals: augment request path to emit a lightweight KV-heat metric (per-tenant, per-model, hashed context window). Heat is aggregated into short-lived time buckets to indicate residency importance.
2) Warmth Manager: controller that ingests KV heat + recent request rates + cold-start metrics and makes decisions to: prewarm model instances, pin KV slices to warm instances, or request temporary memory reservations.
3) Tenant Cache Fencing: soft-fence tokens that mark KV slices as high-priority for a tenant for a duration. Fences prevent low-priority evictions by opportunistic tenants and are revocable by the Warmth Manager based on confidence.
4) Autoscaler integration: autoscaler receives a multi-component demand signal: compute demand, KV-heating demand, and memory-residency demand. Autoscaler policies include short-window microburst lanes and longer warm-reservation lanes.
5) Fallbacks: on failure or low confidence warm manager falls back to existing capacity pools and graceful-degradation lanes (quantized model variants or reduced fidelity outputs).

Component details
- KV heat collector (runtime hook): tiny shim that records per-request keys/hashed prefixes, counts repeated access. Export via metrics (prom/gRPC) with TTL to prevent long-term retention. Privacy: do not export raw keys; only hashed aggregates and counts.
- Warmth Manager (controller): stateless decision engine (k-snapshot windowing) that emits actions: PREWARM, PIN_KV_SLICE, EVICT_PIN, REQUEST_MEMORY_RESERVATION. Runs in control plane with a short RTO (~1s–5s).
- Fencing token API: tokens are capability objects tied to a tenant and model version with TTL; they are attached to instance-level eviction policies. Ops can revoke or extend tokens via controller API.
- Autoscaler changes: accept heat-derived signals and expose new scaling knobs: microburst-provision, transient-memory-reserve, fence-priority-weight. Scaling decisions should maintain latency SLOs while minimizing sustained cost.

SLOs and metrics
- Primary SLO: p99 generation latency (KV-heavy) <= baseline * 0.75 for instrumented tenants within 30s after rollout.
- Secondary: rate of cross-tenant eviction events should decrease by 60% in test clusters.
- Telemetry: heat-score per tenant, number of active fences, fence hit/miss ratio, warm-start time reduction, memory reservation usage, autoscaler scaling decisions and cost delta.

Rollout plan
1) Canary instrumentation: introduce KV heat collector in canary runtime (internal-only tenants). Collect data for 2–4 weeks.
2) Warmth Manager alpha: deploy controller without enforcement, only surfacing suggested actions to ops dashboard. Validate decisions against historical outcomes.
3) Soft-fence beta: implement fence tokens but default TTL very short and enforcement only on dedicated canaries. Monitor eviction delta.
4) Autoscaler integration: enable autoscaler to consider heat signals in beta pools. Run in observation-first mode for 1–2 weeks.
5) Gradual enable: allow product to opt tenants into fence benefits; provide cost insights.

Operational playbook (short)
- Detect: alert when fence-hit ratio drops or when p99 increases > 15% for instrumented tenant.
- Verify: check heat-score trend and warm-pool activity. Correlate with tenant spike traces and eviction logs.
- Mitigate: temporarily revoke low-priority fences, scale up warm pool, or shift tenant to dedicated hot-lane.
- Postmortem: record whether fences prevented or contributed to any capacity conflicts; add mitigating rules if necessary.

Security and privacy considerations
- Keys and content must never leave the runtime in plaintext. Heat signals are aggregated hashed counters only.
- Access to fence token management APIs gated by enterprise RBAC and audited.

Risks and trade-offs
- Overfencing: too many fences reduce multiplexing efficiency and increase cost. Need conservative token issuance heuristics.
- Signal noise: noisy heat signals may cause flip-flopping; require smoothing and minimum hold times.
- Complexity: adds a control loop that interacts with autoscaler and eviction logic—must be thoroughly tested to avoid oscillation.

Open questions / decisions to make
- TTL defaults: what reasonable default fence TTL balances stability vs. responsiveness? (30s vs 5m?)
- Scoring function: how to combine heat, request rate, and model cold-start cost into a single actionable score?
- Cost attribution: how to reflect warm-pool memory reservations and fence-afforded isolation in billing?
- Tenant opt-in UX: should this be automatic for latency SLA customers or opt-in via console?

Next steps / immediate action items
- Product: define initial fence TTL recommendation and opt-in policy (Assignee: Evelyn) — due 2025-01-20.
- Eng (runtime): prototype KV heat collector and exports (Assignee: Ravi) — POC by 2025-02-03.
- Eng (control plane): implement Warmth Manager skeleton and fence token API (Assignee: Luis) — alpha by 2025-02-24.
- Observability: dashboard templated with heat-score, fence inventory, and warm-pool health (Assignee: Maya) — dashboard by 2025-02-10.

Notes to reviewers
- This sketch intentionally focuses on KV heat and soft fencing as a complement to many existing burst-credit and warm-pool ideas. It is meant to be a narrower, implementable first step that can reduce latency tails for critical tenants without wholesale changes to reservation/burst economics.
- Please call out any operational failure modes we missed and suggest safe defaults for TTLs and scoring thresholds.

References and related work
- Related internal PRD: confluence:DEDICATED-CAPACITY-BURST-ECO (see link).
- Prior experiments: github:infra/benchmarks/kv-eviction-sim-jan2024.
- Slack thread: #dedicated-autoscale (search thread: "kv heat pilot").
